# Regulation and Spectrum {.session-marker}

- Spectrum allocation and licensing.
- Frequency band characteristics.
- Emission limits and exposure constraints.
- Coverage obligations.
- Infrastructure and spectrum sharing.

## Why this session now

- Sessions 1 to 5 defined the demand, radio design, transport architecture, cost structure, and energy implications.
- Before rollout, the system must still clear national authorization, international coordination, equipment certification, and launch approval.
- In this session, **coverage** should be read as regulatory or commercial service reach unless the slide says **radio** or **service** coverage explicitly.

## Regulatory agencies

| Body | Scope | Main role for NTN |
|:--|:--|:--|
| ITU | Global | Coordinates spectrum and orbital-resource use across administrations |
| National regulator, e.g. FCC | Country | Authorizes operation, market access, and national spectrum use |
| Regional standards or certification bodies, e.g. ETSI | Regional market | Translate regulatory requirements into testing and equipment compliance processes |
| 3GPP | Global standardization | Defines how NTN integrates with the 5G system, but does not grant licenses |

## Licensing process

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["P1<br/>Pre-filing"] --> B["P2<br/>National authorization"]
    A --> C["P3<br/>ITU coordination"]
    A --> D["P4<br/>Equipment certification"]
    B --> E["P5<br/>Launch and initial service"]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    B --> F["P6<br/>5G integration and partnerships"]
    F --> E
```
## Licensing process

| Phase | Main question | Typical output |
|:--|:--|:--|
| P1 Pre-filing | Is the proposed service technically and commercially coherent? | Baseline mission, target band, initial link-budget and coverage assumptions |
| P2 National authorization | Can we operate this service in a given country? | National operating authorization with conditions |
| P3 ITU coordination | Can this system coexist internationally with other filings? | Filing visibility, coordination path, and long-term spectrum protection |
| P4 Equipment certification | Do terminals and gateways satisfy market rules? | Certified devices and gateway equipment |
| P5 Launch and initial service | Can we launch safely and activate a compliant first service? | In-orbit validation and controlled initial operation |
| P6 5G integration | Can the system interwork with mobile operators and the 5G core? | Roaming, charging, core integration, and commercial readiness |

## National authorization vs ITU coordination

| Aspect | National authorization | ITU coordination |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Decision maker | Country regulator | National administration interacting with ITU |
| Main concern | Domestic permission to operate | International interference management |
| Output | License, market access, or operating approval | Filing record, coordination, and eventual MIFR entry |
| Time logic | Needed before service in that country | Runs in parallel and can outlast first service launch |
| Student shortcut | "Can I serve users here?" | "Can I keep using this spectrum internationally?" |

### P1: Pre-filing

**Pre-filing phase objective**: turn a service idea into a licensable technical concept.

- Define the intended service: \acr{D2D}, IoT, fixed broadband, backhaul, emergency messaging...
- Define the target geography, expected users, throughput, availability, latency, and continuity requirements.
- Choose the space segment: \acr{LEO}, \acr{MEO}, \acr{GEO}, \acr{HAPS}
- Type of architecture (transparent or regenerative)

**Pre-filing phase deliverables**: regulatory strategy approved, so national and international filings can start in parallel.

### P1: Technical feasibility

"*Can the proposed service meet its target performance with proposed spacecraft, terminals, gateways, and spectrum?*"

- Perform a link budget for the forward link and return link.
- Evaluate Doppler, propagation delay, atmospheric loss, clutter, antenna pointing, and availability.
- Size the constellation and gateway network for coverage and capacity.
- Identify whether a single satellite can support the promised “initial service” or only a demonstration / geographically limited service.

### P1: Spectrum strategy

Objective: select bands that are physically suitable, legally available, and supported by equipment.

- Start with the ITU allocation table: determine whether the band supports the proposed radio service.
- Map the regulatory allocation to a usable 3GPP NTN operating band and to the target region.
- Assess the trade-off between lower-band coverage robustness and higher-band bandwidth.
- Identify co-primary services and incumbent users that may trigger coordination or constrain emissions.

### P2: National Authorization

**Objective**: obtain permission from the national regulator to operate a space station, earth station, satellite service, or market-access service.

- National authorisation is jurisdiction-specific: e.g. FCC  is relevant to the US, while ETSI is relevant in Europe.
- The regulator examines public-interest issues, spectrum compatibility, technical parameters, ownership/security requirements, and debris mitigation.

**Inputs**: evidence for the regulator to assess compatibility and compliance (output of phase 1)

### P2: National Authorization result

Once the application is approved:

- The operator has authority to proceed under explicit technical and operational conditions.
- International coordination, equipment authorisation, launch approvals, and host-country market access may still be required.
- The operator should treat the authorisation as a controlled baseline: material changes in orbit, frequency, EIRP, or service may require modification.

::: {.callout-important}
The licence does not automatically authorise service in every country.
:::

### P3: ITU filing

**Objective**: secure internationally recognised use of spectrum and associated orbital resources while managing cross-border interference.

- The ITU does not license a private operator directly; the relevant national administration submits the filing.
- The process makes planned networks visible to other administrations and identifies cases requiring coordination.
- It is a spectrum-rights and interference-management process, distinct from a domestic operating licence.
- Bilateral coordination can be time-consuming.

### P3: ITU filing result

- Successful filing results in a “notification” of the planned network, which is published in the ITU Master Register.
- A successful entry in the \acr{MIFR}
- *ITU 7-year deadline*: you have 7 years from the **Advance Publication Information (API)** filing to launch one satellite.

::: {.callout-note}
Launching a satellite, national authorisation, and final MIFR recording (ITU coordination) are related—but separate—events
:::

### P4: Equipment certification

**Objective**: show that terminals, gateways, and radio equipment meet the technical rules applicable to the markets in which they are sold or operated.

In particular, for RF equipment, the certification process verifies:

- Transmitted power and occupied bandwidth.
- Adjacent-channel leakage and emissions outside the authorised band.
- Receiver sensitivity, blocking, and immunity to unwanted signals.
- Antenna radiation performance and, where applicable, NTN-specific motion effects.

### P4: NTN-specific device and network testing

The following aspects are specifically relevant to NTN equipment:

- Spectrum **leakage** due to Doppler and motion of the satellite (especially for \acr{LEO} and \acr{MEO}).
- Satellites and gateways may impose different **uplink power and antenna constraints** than terrestrial base stations.
- Direct-to-device operation requires realistic evaluation of handset antennas, body loss, and low elevation angles.

### P5: Launch and initial service

**Objective**: obtain the right to launch and demonstrate readiness to place the spacecraft into its planned orbit.

- Launch authorisation is separate from spectrum licensing.
- The launch authority evaluates public safety, environmental and security considerations, and the launch operator’s compliance.
- The spacecraft must satisfy the launch provider’s mechanical, electrical, safety, and interface requirements.
- The operator needs insurance, a launch contract, mission operations procedures, and contingency plans.

### P5: IOV, activation and decomissioning

- \acr{IOV} aims at proving that the actual satellite system behaves within its technical and regulatory envelope. This includes: orbit, RF performance, link budget, and service quality.
- The activation moves from technical demonstration to a controlled, commercially usable initial service.
- Regarding decommissioning, the operator must demonstrate that the satellite can be safely de-orbited or moved to a graveyard orbit at the end of its life.
  - Debris mitigation is not an afterthought: it must be designed, financed, monitored, and reported throughout the mission.

### P6: 5G NTN integration

**Objective**: make the satellite access network behave as an extension of the 5G system rather than as an isolated overlay.

- Implement the applicable 3GPP NTN features in the UE, radio access network, gateway, and 5G Core.
- Integrate authentication, policy, charging, roaming, emergency-service handling, and observability.
- Support appropriate mobility behaviour between terrestrial and satellite coverage.
- Align the technical architecture with the chosen commercial model: satellite operator, \acr{MNO} partner, wholesale provider, or joint offering.

## Licensing timeline for Starlink {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

| Date     | Milestone                                         | Time from Start |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Nov 2016 | FCC application filed (4,425 satellites)          | Month 0         |
| Mar 2018 | **FCC authorization granted**                     | **~16 months**      |
| Feb 2018 | First test satellites (Tintin A/B) launched       | ~15 months      |
| May 2019 | First operational batch (60 satellites) launched  | ~30 months      |
| Oct 2020 | Public beta service launched                      | ~48 months      |
| 2026     | 15,000+ satellites authorized, thousands deployed | 10 years        |

### Starlink spectrum filings {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

Info extracted from Space Exploration Holdings, LLC (Starlink) FCC regulatory filings

| Frequency range | Band | Typical NTN role | Why it matters |
|:--:|:--:|:--|:--|
| 10700 - 14500 | Ku | User access and some gateway links | Stronger propagation than higher bands, but less total bandwidth |
| 17800 - 30000 | Ka | High-capacity user and feeder links | More bandwidth, but greater sensitivity to atmospheric loss |
| 37500 - 52400 | V | Future high-capacity feeder or backhaul use | Very large bandwidth, but stricter propagation and equipment constraints |
| 71000 - 76000 | V | Experimental or high-capacity backbone use | Attractive capacity, but demanding RF implementation |
| 76000 - 86000 | W | Very high-frequency backhaul or feeder use | Highest bandwidth potential, highest atmospheric penalty |
